title: How Narco States Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain narco states: countries or regions where the government either tolerates, participates in, or is controlled by drug trafficking. They cover how narco states form (weakened government, bribery, compromised intelligence services, civil war leftovers, poverty, money), the role of Cold War proxy wars in Central America, US policy missteps (Noriega, School of the Americas, Afghanistan poppy eradication), and the rise of West Africa as a cocaine transit hub, especially Guinea-Bissau. The episode ends with listener mail from Lisa about UK DNA database collection after a conductor was spat on.

segments.title: Opening banter and definition
segments.summary: Hosts introduce narco states, with Chuck giving a working definition: a country or region where the government allows or participates in drug trafficking. They note such states are usually a region or city rather than a whole country.

segments.title: Drug routes and Mexico border violence
segments.summary: They discuss Juarez's rising murder rate after 2007 and how the closing of the Caribbean route in the 1990s pushed cocaine through Central America and Mexico. They also note US and European drug consumption and the high street price markup of cocaine in Moscow.

segments.title: The social contract and the state monopoly on violence
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck explain Hobbes's social contract and the state's monopoly on violence, and how a narco state turns that contract into a sham when the government serves drug traffickers instead of citizens.

segments.title: How narco states form: intimidation, bribery and compromised intelligence
segments.summary: They describe the routes to a narco state: judges and politicians killed by traffickers, the FARC attack on Colombia's justice building, bribery of politicians, and compromised intelligence services that turn the military. Smuggling expertise from intelligence services is also noted.

segments.title: Instability, civil wars and poverty
segments.summary: They argue that long civil wars in Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua left weak infrastructure, many guns and unemployed veterans, and that poor countries with these conditions are easily pulled into narco states.

segments.title: Afghanistan, poppies and aerial eradication
segments.summary: Afghanistan's economy relies heavily on heroin, with reports of record poppy harvests and officials tied to drug lords. Hosts describe the dispute over aerial spraying versus hand eradication, and contrast it with Colombia's use of spraying against coca.

segments.title: Corruption in Guatemala and Central America
segments.summary: They describe a Guatemalan federal judge accused of taking bribes to dismiss a drug case, legislation that blocks extradition, and the high ratio of illegal guns to legal ones in Central America.

segments.title: Cold War proxies, US training and Noriega
segments.summary: They explain how the US and USSR fought proxy wars in Central and South America, leaving trained fighters and weapons behind. They discuss US-backed groups such as Lacka Frida, the School of the Americas training of later cartel leaders, the War on Drugs paradox in the 1980s, and Manuel Noriega's CIA ties and eventual capture in Panama.

segments.title: Africa and the Guinea-Bissau narco state
segments.summary: Hosts trace the rise of drugs in Africa from Zambia's marijuana trade in the 1980s and Senegal in the 1990s to West Africa's role as a cocaine route to Europe. Guinea-Bissau is described as a near-complete narco state, where fishermen found cocaine packages, a military faction seized seized cocaine from police, and the president was assassinated.

segments.title: Wrap-up and plug
segments.summary: Chuck says the article is worth reading and points listeners to the HowStuffWorks search for Narco States. The hosts briefly discuss the episode and sign off.

segments.title: Listener mail: UK DNA exclusion samples
segments.summary: Lisa, a train engineer in England, writes that British Transport Police pressed a conductor for a DNA sample for exclusion purposes after he was spat on, and he refused, so the offender went unpunished. Josh and Chuck share their own spitting anecdotes.
